stem: The chapter 'Colonialism and the Countryside' examines how British colonial rule affected rural India, using especially the __________ of the colonial state.
options: Official records and archives (revenue records, surveys, reports)
solution: The chapter examines the impact of British colonial rule on the Indian countryside, and it does so especially by exploring the OFFICIAL RECORDS and archives generated by the colonial state — revenue records, surveys, settlement reports, enquiry commission reports, and the like. A key sub-theme is learning how to read these official sources critically (since they reflect the colonial administration's viewpoint and purposes). So the chapter draws especially on the official records/archives of the colonial state.

stem: The 'Permanent Settlement', a major land-revenue system introduced by the British in 1793 in Bengal (and Bihar), was associated especially with which Governor-General?
solution: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 in Bengal (and Bihar, and later parts of Orissa and Banaras) under the Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. Under it, the revenue to be paid to the state was fixed PERMANENTLY (it was not to be increased in future), and this settlement was made with the ZAMINDARS, who were recognised as the proprietors of the land and were responsible for paying the fixed revenue. So the Permanent Settlement (1793) is associated with Lord Cornwallis.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the revenue was fixed permanently and the settlement was made with the __________, who were made responsible for paying it.
solution: Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the settlement was made with the ZAMINDARS. The zamindars were recognised as the proprietors of the land (with hereditary, saleable rights) and were made responsible for collecting rent from the peasants and paying a PERMANENTLY FIXED amount of revenue to the Company/state. The idea was that a fixed, permanent demand would give zamindars security and an incentive to improve their estates. So the settlement was made with the zamindars.

stem: A key term of the Permanent Settlement was the 'Sunset Law', which stipulated that __________.
options: If a zamindar failed to pay the fixed revenue by the sunset of a specified date, his estate (or part of it) could be auctioned/sold off
Zamindars could only collect rent after sunset
The sun would set the revenue rate
Peasants had to work only until sunset
solution: The 'Sunset Law' was a strict condition of the Permanent Settlement: if a zamindar FAILED to pay the fixed revenue amount in full by the SUNSET of a specified due date, his estate (or a portion of it) could be seized and AUCTIONED/SOLD off by the Company to recover the dues. This rigid rule put enormous pressure on zamindars, and especially in the early decades many defaulted (for various reasons) and lost their estates at auction. So the Sunset Law provided for the auction of a defaulting zamindar's estate. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: In the early years of the Permanent Settlement, many zamindars failed to pay the fixed revenue and lost their lands. This was partly because __________.
options: The revenue demand was fixed very high (and was rigid/inflexible even in bad harvest years), zamindars' own power to collect from ryots was initially curtailed, and prices were often low
There were no peasants to collect rent from
Zamindars refused all payment out of protest
solution: In the early decades of the Permanent Settlement, many zamindars defaulted and lost their estates for several reasons: the initial revenue demand was fixed very HIGH (in the expectation of future agricultural expansion), and it was RIGID/INFLEXIBLE — the same fixed sum had to be paid even in years of poor harvests or low prices; agricultural prices were often depressed in this early period, reducing zamindars' income; and the Company's regulations initially LIMITED the zamindars' own power to coerce rent from the ryots (e.g., restricting their judicial/policing powers). These pressures caused widespread default and the auctioning of estates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The zamindars devised various strategies to avoid losing their estates at auction. One such device was __________.
options: Fictitious/benami sales and manipulation of auctions (e.g., women of the household or servants bidding, or agents buying back the estate)
solution: To survive the harsh terms of the settlement and avoid genuinely losing their estates at auction, zamindars devised various strategies and manipulations. One notable device was resorting to FICTITIOUS/benami sales and manipulating the auctions: for example, the zamindar's own agents, servants, or even the women of his household would put in bids and 'buy' the estate at the auction (so it stayed in the family's control), or agents would refuse to pay so the estate could be bought back cheaply, or dues would be transferred among family members. Through such manoeuvres, many zamindars managed to retain effective control of their estates. So one device was fictitious/benami auction manipulation.

stem: The area around Bengal known for a great uprising of tribal peasants against moneylenders and the colonial order, discussed in the chapter, is associated with the __________.
options: Santhals (the Santhal rebellion of 1855–56) and the region of Rajmahal hills / 'Damin-i-Koh'
solution: The chapter discusses the Santhals — a tribal/adivasi people — and their great uprising, the Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56, against the oppression of moneylenders (dikus), zamindars, and the colonial authorities. The Santhals had been settled in a demarcated tract of the Rajmahal hills area known as the 'Damin-i-Koh' ('skirts of the hills'), where they cleared forest and cultivated, but they came to be exploited by moneylenders and traders and burdened by revenue, leading to their revolt. So the uprising is associated with the Santhals and the Rajmahal hills/Damin-i-Koh.

stem: The Santhals were settled by the colonial authorities in a demarcated forest tract called the 'Damin-i-Koh'. There they were expected to __________.
options: Clear the forest and practise settled cultivation (becoming settled peasants who would pay revenue)
solution: The colonial authorities demarcated a tract of land in the Rajmahal hills region — the 'Damin-i-Koh' — and settled the Santhals there, expecting them to CLEAR the forest and take up SETTLED (plough) CULTIVATION, transforming into settled peasants who would expand the arable and pay land revenue to the state. The Santhals did clear forests and cultivate, but they were soon squeezed by high revenue demands, and above all by exploitative moneylenders and traders (dikus) who trapped them in debt and seized their lands — grievances that led to the 1855–56 rebellion. So they were settled to clear forest and practise settled cultivation.

stem: The moneylenders and traders whom the Santhals blamed for their oppression (and against whom they revolted) were referred to as __________.
solution: The Santhals referred to the moneylenders, traders, and outsiders who exploited them — trapping them in debt at exorbitant interest, cheating them, and seizing their lands and produce — as 'dikus' (meaning 'outsiders'). Resentment against the dikus (along with oppressive zamindars, the police, and the colonial revenue burden) was a central grievance behind the Santhal rebellion of 1855–56. So the exploitative moneylenders/outsiders were the dikus. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: The Santhal rebellion (1855–56) was led by the brothers __________.
options: Sidhu and Kanhu (Sido and Kanhu Murmu)
solution: The Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56 was led by the brothers Sidhu (Sido) and Kanhu (Kanhu) Murmu, along with their brothers Chand and Bhairav. They mobilised thousands of Santhals to rise up against the dikus (moneylenders/traders), the zamindars, and the colonial authorities, aiming to end their oppression and establish their own rule/just order. The rebellion was eventually suppressed with much bloodshed by the British. So the leaders were Sidhu and Kanhu. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Fifth Report, an important colonial document referred to in the chapter, was __________.
options: A report submitted to the British Parliament in 1813 on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India (including revenue and the state of the countryside)
solution: The 'Fifth Report' was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the English East India Company in India, submitted to the BRITISH PARLIAMENT in 1813. It was a voluminous document (running to over a thousand pages) containing information and appendices on the revenue system, the condition of the countryside, the zamindars and ryots, petitions, and reports of collectors and officials. It became an influential source shaping perceptions of Company rule in India — though historians read it critically, aware of its context (it was produced partly in the context of debates in Britain over the Company's monopoly and conduct). So the Fifth Report was a 1813 report to the British Parliament.

stem: Historians caution that the Fifth Report, though valuable, must be read critically because it __________.
options: Was shaped by the political context in Britain (debates over the Company) and tended to exaggerate the decline/mismanagement to serve particular arguments; and it reflected an official viewpoint
Was purely fictional with no basis
solution: Historians caution that the Fifth Report, while a rich source, must be read CRITICALLY. It was produced within a particular POLITICAL context in Britain — there were vigorous debates about the East India Company (including attacks on its monopoly and its conduct in India), and those who compiled and used the Report had their own agendas. As a result, the Report tended to EXAGGERATE the decline of local society and the mismanagement/oppression under the Company (and under the older zamindari order) to serve certain arguments, and it reflected an official, outsider viewpoint. So it must be read with awareness of its context and biases. So option 1 is correct. This is a key methodological point about using colonial records.

stem: In the Bombay Deccan, the British introduced a different revenue system (not the Permanent Settlement) in which the revenue was settled directly with individual cultivators (ryots). This was the __________.
solution: In the Bombay Deccan (and much of southern and western India), the British introduced the RYOTWARI system, in which the revenue settlement was made DIRECTLY with the individual cultivators (the ryots) rather than with zamindars. Each ryot was held responsible for paying revenue on his own holding, the land was surveyed and assessed, and the revenue was periodically revised (not fixed permanently). This system is the backdrop to the chapter's discussion of the Deccan ryots, their indebtedness, and the Deccan Riots. So the Deccan system was the ryotwari system.

stem: Under the ryotwari system in the Deccan, the revenue demand was __________ (unlike the Permanent Settlement).
options: Not fixed permanently — it was periodically revised (re-assessed), and was often set quite high
Paid only in kind, never in cash
solution: Unlike the Permanent Settlement (where the demand was fixed forever), the ryotwari system involved a revenue demand that was NOT permanent: it was periodically REVISED/re-assessed (e.g., every thirty years in some settlements), and it was often set quite HIGH. The high and revisable demand, collected rigidly even in bad years and payable in cash, placed heavy pressure on the Deccan ryots, pushing many into debt with moneylenders — a background cause of the Deccan Riots. So the ryotwari demand was periodically revised and often high. This contrast with the Permanent Settlement is important.

stem: The great agrarian uprising of 1875 in the Bombay Deccan, in which peasants (ryots) attacked moneylenders and destroyed their debt-bonds, is known as the __________.
solution: The Deccan Riots of 1875 were a major agrarian uprising in the Bombay Deccan (beginning in Pune/Poona district, e.g., at Supa, and spreading), in which the ryots (peasants) rose up against the moneylenders (sahukars), attacking them, and seizing and DESTROYING the bonds, deeds, and account-books that recorded their debts (and sometimes burning down houses and shops). The immediate targets were the moneylenders whom the peasants blamed for their oppression and dispossession. So the 1875 uprising is the Deccan Riots. A Deccan Riots Commission was appointed to enquire into its causes.

stem: A major underlying cause of the Deccan Riots was the peasants' mounting __________ to moneylenders.
options: Indebtedness (debt) — ryots had fallen deeply into debt, losing land and dignity to the sahukars
solution: A major underlying cause of the Deccan Riots was the mounting INDEBTEDNESS of the ryots to the moneylenders (sahukars). Squeezed by the high, rigid, cash revenue demand of the ryotwari system, and needing loans (especially after bad harvests and during a slump), the peasants borrowed from moneylenders, who charged high interest, manipulated accounts and bonds, and increasingly seized the peasants' land, produce, and property when debts could not be repaid. The peasants' sense of being cheated and dispossessed, and their resentment at losing land and dignity, boiled over into the attacks on moneylenders. So the underlying cause was peasant indebtedness to moneylenders.

stem: The peasants' anger against the moneylenders in the Deccan intensified after the __________, which had first raised and then collapsed cotton prices/incomes.
options: End of the American Civil War (the cotton boom collapsed around 1865, hurting Deccan cotton growers)
solution: The peasants' distress and anger in the Deccan were intensified by the cotton cycle linked to the American Civil War (1861–65). During the war, cotton exports from the American South were disrupted, so Britain turned to Indian (Deccan) cotton — causing a BOOM: cotton prices and demand soared, and Deccan cotton growers (and moneylenders) expanded credit and cultivation. But when the American Civil War ENDED (around 1865), American cotton returned to the market, the boom COLLAPSED, prices and exports crashed, and Deccan cotton growers' incomes fell sharply — leaving them unable to repay the debts contracted during the boom. This bust deepened indebtedness and grievance, feeding into the 1875 riots. So the trigger was the end of the American Civil War and the cotton price collapse.

stem: After the Deccan Riots, the government appointed a commission to investigate. This shows that the colonial state responded to unrest by __________.
options: Setting up enquiry commissions (like the Deccan Riots Commission) whose reports became sources historians use — while reflecting official concerns and perspectives
solution: In response to the Deccan Riots, the colonial government appointed the Deccan Riots Commission to investigate the causes of the unrest. The Commission gathered evidence — statements from ryots, moneylenders, and officials, and reports and statistics — and produced a report. Such enquiry-commission reports became valuable SOURCES that historians use to reconstruct rural conditions and grievances. However, historians read them critically, because they reflect the OFFICIAL concerns and perspective of the colonial state (for instance, the Commission was keen to establish whether the government's own revenue demand was to blame, and tended to shift blame onto the moneylenders). So the state responded via enquiry commissions whose reports are useful but partial sources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Deccan Riots Commission's report tended to __________, reflecting the colonial government's reluctance to blame its own policies.
options: Place the blame primarily on the moneylenders, while downplaying the role of the government's high revenue demand
solution: The Deccan Riots Commission's report tended to place the blame for the peasants' distress primarily on the MONEYLENDERS (the sahukars) and their exploitative practices, while DOWNPLAYING or denying the role of the GOVERNMENT's own high revenue demand in impoverishing the ryots. This reflected the colonial government's reluctance to hold its own revenue policy responsible for the unrest. Historians therefore read the report critically, recognising this bias, and use it (along with other evidence) to reconstruct the real causes — which included both the moneylenders' exploitation and the heavy state demand. So the report shifted blame onto the moneylenders and away from government policy. This is a key point about reading official records critically.

stem: Which broad point about COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS does the chapter emphasise?
options: They are neutral, complete, and perfectly objective

They are valuable but must be read critically — they were produced by the colonial administration for its own purposes, reflect official perspectives and biases, and often obscure the viewpoints of peasants and other ordinary people
They contain no useful information at all
They were written by the peasants themselves
solution: A central methodological point of the chapter is that COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS (revenue records, surveys, reports like the Fifth Report and the Deccan Riots Commission report) are extremely VALUABLE sources — but they must be read CRITICALLY. They were produced by the colonial administration for its OWN purposes (chiefly revenue collection and control), and they inevitably reflect the OFFICIAL perspective, assumptions, and biases of the colonial state (and of those who compiled them). Crucially, they often OBSCURE or distort the viewpoints, experiences, and voices of the peasants and other ordinary rural people. So historians must interrogate these records carefully — reading 'against the grain', corroborating with other evidence, and being alert to what is left out. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The Permanent Settlement, by making the revenue demand fixed and permanent, was expected by the British to __________ — though the results were mixed.
options: Give zamindars a secure incentive to invest in and improve agriculture (and provide the state with a stable, assured income)
solution: The British EXPECTED the Permanent Settlement to bring several benefits: by fixing the revenue demand PERMANENTLY, it would give the zamindars security and a strong INCENTIVE to invest in and IMPROVE their estates and agriculture (since any increase in produce/income above the fixed demand would be theirs to keep), thereby raising agricultural productivity; and it would give the STATE a STABLE, ASSURED income (a fixed sum) and create a loyal class of landed proprietors. In practice, however, the RESULTS were MIXED and often disappointing: many zamindars initially defaulted and lost their estates, the expected agricultural improvement was often not realised, the rigidity hurt in bad years, and the burden was passed onto the ryots. So the intention was to give zamindars an incentive to improve and give the state stable income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the ultimate burden of the revenue demand often fell on the __________, who were squeezed by the zamindars.
options: Ryots (peasants/cultivators), through high rents and various cesses
solution: Although the Permanent Settlement was made with the zamindars, the ultimate BURDEN of the revenue demand often fell on the RYOTS (the actual peasant cultivators). To meet the fixed revenue payable to the state (and to profit), zamindars extracted high RENTS and various additional cesses/levies from the peasants, and could evict or coerce them. The peasants thus bore the weight of the system, often with little security of tenure and subject to exactions. So the burden fell on the ryots. This shows how the settlement, made with zamindars, ultimately pressed down on the cultivators.

stem: The term 'jotedars', mentioned in the context of Bengal's countryside, refers to __________.
options: Rich peasants/landholders who controlled large areas, lent money, and grew powerful in the villages (sometimes at the expense of the zamindars)
solution: In the Bengal countryside, the jotedars were a class of RICH PEASANTS/landholders who, over time, acquired control of large areas of land, dominated local trade and moneylending, and grew POWERFUL in the villages. As many zamindars (especially absentee ones) weakened under the pressures of the Permanent Settlement, the jotedars — being resident and locally rooted — often gained at the zamindars' expense, controlling the actual cultivators (many of whom were their sharecroppers/adhiyars), resisting the zamindars' demands, and even acquiring zamindari lands at auctions. They represent an important rural power group that rose under colonial conditions. So jotedars were rich, powerful village landholders. This is a prelims-relevant term.

stem: The jotedars were often more powerful than the zamindars in the actual villages because they __________.
options: Were resident in the countryside (not absentee), directly controlled the cultivators and local trade/credit, and could resist the zamindars' demands
Owned the British East India Company
solution: The jotedars were often more powerful than the zamindars WITHIN the villages because: they were RESIDENT in the countryside (whereas many zamindars were absentee, living in towns), giving them direct, on-the-ground control; they directly controlled a large body of poorer cultivators and SHARECROPPERS (adhiyars/bargadars, who cultivated the jotedars' land and gave a share of the produce); they dominated local TRADE and MONEYLENDING; and they were well-placed to RESIST the zamindars' demands for revenue/rent and to frustrate their authority (even buying up zamindari estates when these were auctioned). This local rootedness and control made them formidable. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rich peasants and moneylenders who exploited the ryots, and the strategies of zamindars and jotedars, together show that colonialism reshaped rural society by __________.
options: Creating new pressures and opportunities that produced winners and losers — strengthening some groups (like certain moneylenders and rich peasants/jotedars) while impoverishing and dispossessing many ordinary peasants and tribal cultivators
solution: The various developments the chapter traces — the fortunes of zamindars under the Permanent Settlement, the rise of jotedars, the indebtedness and dispossession of Deccan ryots to moneylenders, and the exploitation and revolt of the Santhals — together show that COLONIALISM RESHAPED rural society by creating new economic and administrative pressures AND opportunities that produced WINNERS and LOSERS. Some groups (certain moneylenders, rich peasants/jotedars, and surviving/adaptive zamindars) gained power and wealth, while many ordinary peasants and tribal cultivators were impoverished, indebted, and dispossessed — sometimes to the point of rebellion. Rural society was thus transformed, differentiated, and often destabilised (not made equal or left unchanged). So option 2 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Many Bengal zamindars lost their estates in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement. Reason (R): The revenue demand was fixed very high and had to be paid rigidly by a fixed date (the Sunset Law), regardless of harvests or prices. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that many Bengal zamindars lost their estates (through auction) in the early decades of the Permanent Settlement. And the reason is (R) that the revenue demand was fixed very HIGH and had to be paid RIGIDLY and in full by a fixed due date under the Sunset Law — regardless of whether the harvest was good or bad, or prices high or low — so that any failure to pay on time led to the estate being auctioned. This harsh, inflexible fiscal regime (together with low prices and curbs on zamindars' collecting power) directly caused the widespread defaults and loss of estates (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Deccan ryots attacked moneylenders and burnt their bonds and deeds in 1875. Reason (R): The peasants saw the moneylenders' account-books and debt-bonds as instruments of their oppression and dispossession. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that during the Deccan Riots of 1875 the ryots attacked the moneylenders and specifically SEIZED and BURNT/destroyed their bonds, deeds, and account-books. And the reason is (R) that the peasants saw these documents — the debt-bonds and manipulated account-books through which the moneylenders enforced debts, extracted exorbitant interest, and seized land — as the very INSTRUMENTS of their oppression and dispossession. By destroying these records, the ryots aimed to wipe out the legal/documentary basis of their debts and the moneylenders' hold over them. So the peasants' view of the bonds as tools of oppression directly explains why they targeted and burnt them (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Colonialism and the Countryside' is that:
options: British rule had no effect on rural India

British colonial rule profoundly transformed the Indian countryside — through revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement in Bengal (fixed demand, settlement with zamindars, the Sunset Law, defaults, and the rise of jotedars) and the ryotwari system in the Deccan (high, revisable demand, ryot indebtedness to moneylenders, and the Deccan Riots of 1875), and through the settlement and exploitation of tribal peoples like the Santhals (leading to their 1855–56 rebellion) — producing winners and losers, deepening indebtedness and dispossession, and provoking resistance; and this history is reconstructed largely from colonial official records (like the Fifth Report and enquiry-commission reports), which are valuable but must be read critically for their official biases
The countryside was prosperous and contented under colonial rule
Only the Mughals affected the countryside
solution: The chapter's overall message is that British colonial rule PROFOUNDLY TRANSFORMED the Indian countryside, in ways that created winners and losers and often deepened rural distress and provoked resistance. In Bengal, the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (under Cornwallis) fixed the revenue permanently and made zamindars the proprietors responsible for paying it under the harsh Sunset Law — leading, in the early decades, to widespread default and the auctioning of estates, various zamindari survival strategies (like fictitious sales), the ultimate burdening of the ryots, and the rise of powerful resident rich peasants (jotedars). In the Bombay Deccan, the ryotwari system imposed a high, revisable cash demand directly on the ryots, who, squeezed further by the collapse of the cotton boom after the American Civil War, fell deep into DEBT to moneylenders (sahukars) and lost land — culminating in the Deccan Riots of 1875, in which peasants attacked moneylenders and burnt their debt-bonds. And in the tribal tracts, peoples like the Santhals were settled (in the Damin-i-Koh) to clear forest and cultivate, but were exploited by dikus (moneylenders/traders) and the revenue burden, rising in the Santhal rebellion (hool) of 1855–56 under Sidhu and Kanhu. Crucially, this whole history is reconstructed largely from COLONIAL OFFICIAL RECORDS — revenue records, surveys, the Fifth Report (1813), and enquiry-commission reports (like the Deccan Riots Commission) — which are invaluable but reflect the OFFICIAL, colonial perspective and biases (often blaming moneylenders while excusing government policy, and obscuring peasants' own voices), and so must be read CRITICALLY. So the overall message is option 2.
